chunks: From him, from Iskab ibn 'Abdah, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr, from his father, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Abu Hamzah, who said:

Abu Khalid al-Kabuli asked Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) about eating the meat of the squirrel and the weasel, and the prayer performed in them. Abu Khalid said, 'The squirrel takes shelter in trees.' He said, 'Then he said: If it has a pathway (sabilah) like the pathway of the cat and the mouse, then its meat is not eaten and prayer in it is not valid.' Then he said, 'As for me, I do not eat it, nor do I forbid it.'

key_terms.السَّبَلَةُ: Pathway or trail (used to distinguish animal types for legal rulings)

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia jurisprudential ruling on eating squirrel and weasel meat and praying in their dwellings?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of distinguishing between wild animals based on their domestic-like characteristics, specifically the presence of a defined pathway (*sabilah*) akin to cats or mice. Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (AS) applies this criterion to exclude squirrels and weasels from permissible consumption and valid prayer spaces, while maintaining a nuanced stance of personal abstention (*war'* ) without imposing strict prohibition (*haram*), reflecting the flexibility in Shia dietary laws regarding wild game.
